claims.text: The starting alloy is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The starting alloy is a simple, single-phase solid solution.
The starting alloy has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The relatively low hardness of the starting alloy is caused by the absence of nanoscale chemical ordering or coherent precipitates.
The relatively low strength of the starting alloy is caused by the absence of nanoscale chemical ordering or coherent precipitates.
Aging at 500–600 °C can induce nanoscale chemical ordering or coherent precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed ordering or precipitation can be induced without altering the alloy's overall phase stability.
Nanoscale chemically ordered regions or coherent precipitates act as dislocation-pinning sites.
The induced nanoscale obstacles create additional barriers to dislocation motion.
Additional barriers to dislocation motion increase hardness.
Additional barriers to dislocation motion increase compressive strength.
Additional barriers to dislocation motion reduce ductility.
In the untreated alloy, the absence of nanoscale obstacles permits easier dislocation glide.
Easier dislocation glide contributes to the favorable plasticity of untreated CoCrFeNiTi.
The heat-treated alloy will have markedly higher hardness than the untreated alloy.
The heat-treated alloy will have markedly higher compressive strength than the untreated alloy.
The heat-treated alloy will have lower ductility than the untreated alloy.
The untreated baseline has moderate hardness and strength with favorable ductility.
The proposed hypothesis is limited to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi aged at 500–600 °C and mechanically tested at room temperature.
Mechanical testing is limited to room-temperature compression at strains up to approximately 5%.

contradictions.description: The intervention explicitly allows coherent precipitate formation, which ordinarily introduces a distinct precipitate phase, while the boundary excludes processing routes that produce multiple phases. The intended distinction between nanoscale precipitation and disallowed multiphase states is not defined.

The falsification rule treats failure to detect ordering or precipitates after aging as falsification of their strengthening role. That result would instead show that the intervention failed to create the proposed mediator and would not by itself contradict the causal mechanism.
